contentSections: Why This Comparison Matters

Aluminium composite panel, commonly called ACP, and engineered metal facade systems are both used to clad the outside of buildings in India, and from the road they can sometimes look similar at first glance. But the two are built very differently, and that difference shows up within a few years of installation, not on day one. Anyone comparing quotes for a home, office or commercial project benefits from understanding exactly what separates the two before signing off on either option, since this is one decision that is expensive and disruptive to reverse once installed.

ACP became popular in India through the 2000s and 2010s because it was affordable, quick to install and gave a clean, flat, modern finish that plaster alone could not achieve. Engineered metal facade systems, using solid aluminium, stainless steel or specially coated panels, have since become the preferred choice for architects and homeowners who want that same clean modern look but with a fundamentally different build quality and a much longer service life.
What Is ACP

ACP is a sandwich panel made of two thin sheets of aluminium, typically around 0.2 to 0.5mm each, bonded to either side of a polymer core, most commonly polyethylene. The thin aluminium skin gives it a metallic appearance and the polymer core keeps it lightweight and easy to cut and bend on site. This combination made it a fast, low-cost way to clad large flat areas of a building, and it remains widely available and commonly used across Indian construction today, particularly on tighter budgets or fast-turnaround commercial fit-outs.
What Is an Engineered Metal Facade System

An engineered metal facade uses solid, single-sheet metal panels, typically aluminium, stainless steel, brass, copper or zinc, formed and finished as a complete structural cladding system rather than a thin decorative skin. Panels are engineered to precise tolerances, mounted on a purpose-built substructure that manages drainage and thermal movement, and finished with an industrial-grade coating such as PVDF, anodising or powder coat, rated to hold colour and integrity for 15 to 30 years depending on the system specified. The design freedom is also considerably wider, ranging from flat cassette panels to fluted, perforated and fully parametric three-dimensional patterns.

Fire Safety: The Most Important Difference

Fire performance is the single most significant difference between the two materials and deserves specific attention rather than being treated as just another line item. Standard ACP with a polyethylene core is combustible, and this specific product category has been directly linked to a number of serious high-rise fire incidents around the world over the past decade, which has led several countries and some Indian states to tighten building code requirements around cladding fire ratings, particularly for taller buildings. Fire-rated ACP variants with a mineral-filled or fire-retardant core do exist and perform considerably better than standard PE-core ACP, but they still contain a polymer element that solid metal panels simply do not have. Engineered metal facade systems, being solid metal with no combustible core, do not carry this specific risk category at all, which is a major reason architects increasingly specify solid metal over ACP for taller buildings, hospitals, hotels and any structure where fire safety compliance is closely scrutinised.
Cost Comparison Over Time

On a pure upfront installed cost basis, ACP is usually the cheaper option, often available from roughly ₹250 to ₹500 per square foot depending on grade and thickness, while engineered metal systems typically range from ₹800 to ₹2,500 per square foot depending on the specific system and finish. Looking only at this initial number makes ACP appear to be the more economical choice, but the comparison changes considerably once the full lifecycle is considered. ACP with a standard finish commonly needs replacement or significant repair within 8 to 15 years as panels fade, edges lift or delamination begins, while a properly coated metal facade is designed to perform for 15 to 30 years with minimal intervention. Over a 20 to 25 year period, a building owner may need to replace ACP cladding once or even twice, each time paying full removal and reinstallation labour on top of new material cost, while a metal facade installed once at a higher initial price can outlast that entire period without replacement.
Why ACP Became So Common in Indian Construction

It helps to understand why ACP spread so widely before comparing it against the alternative. Through the 2000s and 2010s, Indian construction was expanding rapidly, and ACP offered a way to give buildings a modern, glossy, finished look quickly and at a price point far below stone, glass or metal alternatives available at the time. It cuts easily with basic tools, does not require heavy machinery to lift and install, and comes in a wide range of factory colours, which made it attractive to contractors working on tight timelines and tighter budgets. For low-rise structures, temporary installations, interior feature walls and signage, these properties still make ACP a reasonable choice today, and it is not being suggested here that the material has no legitimate use at all.
Where the Two Materials Genuinely Differ in Real Buildings

The gap between ACP and engineered metal becomes most visible a few years after installation rather than on the day the scaffolding comes down. ACP panels are held in place using adhesive bonding between the metal skins and the polymer core, and this bond can weaken over time under sustained heat cycling, particularly on west and south-facing walls that absorb strong afternoon sun for most of the year in Indian cities. Once the bond starts to fail, panel edges lift, corners curl, and moisture can work its way into the core, which accelerates further damage. Solid metal panels have no internal bond to fail in this way, since the entire panel is one continuous piece of material, and the coating sits directly on the metal surface rather than relying on an adhesive layer between two different materials.

Joint and seam detailing is another practical difference installers and architects notice over time. Because ACP is thinner and lighter, panel joints are often sealed with silicone or a simple trim, which can degrade and require resealing periodically. Engineered metal systems typically use a mechanical, concealed fixing and interlocking joint system designed specifically for the coefficient of thermal expansion of solid metal, which tends to hold up with far less periodic maintenance over the life of the building.
What Architects and Building Codes Are Increasingly Requiring

Following several high-profile international fire incidents linked to combustible cladding, many Indian architects and consultants now default to specifying either fire-rated ACP or, increasingly, solid non-combustible metal facades for any building above a certain height, and for building types such as hospitals, hotels, schools and high-density residential towers where evacuation and fire risk carry higher stakes. This shift in professional practice is one of the clearest signals of where the market is heading, since architects specifying material on a project have both liability and professional reputation riding on the choice, and a growing number are choosing to avoid standard PE-core ACP altogether rather than manage the fire rating question project by project.
Which One Should You Choose

• Choose ACP if the project has a very tight budget, a short-term use horizon, or is a temporary or low-rise structure where fire rating requirements are minimal and design longevity is not the priority.
  • Choose an engineered metal facade if the building is residential, commercial, a high-rise, or any structure where long-term appearance, fire safety and total cost of ownership matter more than the lowest possible upfront price.
  • For homes, a metal facade used selectively as an entrance or accent feature is often achievable within a similar budget to a full ACP treatment, since the total area being clad is smaller.
  • For commercial and hospitality projects, most architects today default to solid metal systems specifically because of the fire performance difference and the brand consistency a long-lasting finish provides.
Frequently Asked Questions

Is ACP banned in India?
ACP is not nationally banned in India, but several states and municipal bodies have tightened fire safety norms for cladding on taller buildings following major fire incidents globally, and many architects now specify fire-rated ACP or solid metal alternatives for high-rise and commercial projects as a precaution and for code compliance.

Is metal facade more expensive than ACP?
Yes, on upfront installed cost, engineered metal facade systems are generally more expensive than standard ACP. However, because metal facades typically last 15 to 30 years compared to 8 to 15 years for ACP, the total cost over the life of the building is often comparable or lower with metal once replacement cycles are factored in.

Can ACP be replaced with metal panels on an existing building?
Yes, existing ACP cladding can generally be removed and replaced with an engineered metal system, provided the existing substructure is inspected and, where needed, upgraded to suit the new material and fixing method.

Does metal facade fade in the sun like ACP?
A properly specified metal facade with a PVDF or comparable industrial coating is rated to resist UV fading and chalking for 15 to 30 years, which is considerably longer than the typical fade resistance of standard ACP finishes.
